strengths: Resolves an explicitly posed open problem from Froese et al. (COLT '25) regarding the parameterized complexity of 2-layer ReLU network verification and Lipschitz constant computation, closing several gaps in the parameterized complexity landscape of neural network verification.

Strong, clean technical results: W[1]-hardness (parameterized by input dimension d) for positivity, surjectivity, maximum approximation, zero-function check, zonotope non-containment, and Lp-Lipschitz constant computation (for all p in (0,∞]), together with matching ETH-based running-time lower bounds of n^{Ω(d)}·poly(N) that show the naive enumeration algorithms are essentially optimal.

The core reduction from Multicolored Clique (Section 3) is technically non-trivial: the input dimension must scale linearly with the clique size, which is much harder than standard NP-hardness reductions. The use of Sidon sets to ensure unique edge encoding is elegant, and the homogenization trick to remove biases is a nice technique.

The paper is not purely negative: it provides genuinely useful positive results, including polynomial-time computability of the L1-Lipschitz constant and FPT computability of the L∞-Lipschitz constant for input-convex networks (Proposition 6.3), and a randomized FPT-approximation for norm maximization on zonotopes via subspace embeddings (Theorems 7.1 and 7.2), connecting network verification to computational geometry.

The zonotope containment result is of independent interest beyond machine learning (computational geometry, control, robotics), and the duality-based transfer from network positivity to zonotope non-containment is clearly explained.

Well-structured and clearly written main text with complete proofs in the appendix; honest limitations section; hardness constructions use sparse networks with few non-zero weights per neuron, which strengthens the practical relevance of the negative results.
The paper clearly delineates the 2-layer vs. 3-layer complexity boundary (e.g., zero-function check polynomial for 2-layer vs. W[1]-hard for 3-layer), sharpening previously known results.
weaknesses: Primarily a hardness/complexity paper with worst-case guarantees; the connection to practical network verification is indirect, and the paper itself acknowledges that it gives no guidance on which natural assumptions would circumvent the hardness in practice.

Several results are extensions of known NP-hardness results (Virmaux & Scaman 2018; Jordan & Dimakis 2020; Froese et al. 2025b) to the parameterized setting rather than new problem definitions or algorithmic techniques; the conceptual framework is incremental relative to the line of work it builds on, even though the technical difficulty of parameterized reductions is real.

The positive results (Section 7 randomized approximation via ℓ1 subspace embeddings) have worst-case running time worse than the sampling-based approximation of Shenmaier (2018), so the algorithmic contribution is of limited standalone value; the authors acknowledge this.

A few minor issues: some cited works carry implausible future dates (e.g., Splittgerber 2026, Ganian 2026, arXiv:2602.15499), and the treatment of p ∈ (0,1) in Theorem 6.2 requires a separate, more delicate scaling argument whose presentation is somewhat terse in the main text.
As a purely theoretical paper, its impact on the broader ML community may be moderate; the main audience is the computational complexity / verification sub-community.

strengths: The paper resolves an explicitly posed open problem (Froese et al., COLT '25) by establishing W[1]-hardness with respect to the input dimension d for 2-LAYER RELU POSITIVITY, SURJECTIVITY, Lipschitz constant computation, and zonotope non-containment, thereby settling the parameterized complexity of a broad family of problems.

Beyond W[1]-hardness, the reductions yield ETH-based lower bounds of n^{Ω(d)} · poly(N) that essentially match the known XP enumeration algorithms, giving tight (near-complete) complexity characterizations rather than mere class-membership separations.

The core technical contribution is nontrivial: designing a Multicolored Clique reduction in which the network input dimension scales linearly with the clique size k (via Sidon sets, spike/penalty gadgets, and homogenization), which is precisely the challenge distinguishing parameterized from classical hardness.

The paper is balanced: alongside hardness, it provides genuinely useful positive results, including polynomial-time computability of the L1-Lipschitz constant and FPT computability of the L∞ constant for input convex networks, and a randomized FPT-approximation for norm maximization on zonotopes via subspace embeddings.

Proofs appear complete and careful in the appendix; the constructions are transparent, the writing is clear, and the limitations section is honest about the worst-case, purely theoretical nature of the results.
weaknesses: The hardness techniques, while executed competently, are largely standard for parameterized complexity: Multicolored Clique reductions with selection/verification gadgets. Much of the paper consists of adapting one core reduction to multiple problems, so the perceived novelty depends heavily on how much weight one gives to resolving the specific open problem versus the technical machinery used.

Several derived results feel incremental or low-effort: Theorem 4.5 (surjectivity) falls out almost directly from positive homogeneity of the homogenized network, and Corollaries 4.3, 4.4, and 6.1 are short corollaries of the main construction rather than substantial independent contributions.

The practical significance of the parameterization is debatable. The paper argues that real data lies near low-dimensional submanifolds, but the hardness constructions use adversarial, deliberately engineered networks; the paper itself concedes it 'is not easy to formulate general guidance to circumvent this hardness in practice,' so the connection to actual network verification practice remains indirect.

The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical component whatsoever; even a small illustration of the enumeration-based algorithms or the approximation scheme on concrete instances could have strengthened the paper's relevance to the AI audience.

Some results are reductions via known equivalences rather than new constructions (e.g., zonotope non-containment follows from prior duality results), which somewhat dilutes the sense of depth of the contribution relative to its broad abstract-level claims.

The randomized approximation results (Section 7) are largely re-derivations of known subspace embedding consequences (Bozzai et al., 2023; Cohen & Peng, 2015) with worst-case running times worse than existing sampling-based guarantees of Shenmaier (2018), limiting their standalone value.

strengths: Resolves open problems explicitly posed by Froese et al. (COLT '25) regarding the parameterized complexity of network verification (positivity/surjectivity) and zonotope containment, which is a concrete and verifiable contribution of independent interest to computational geometry, control theory, and robotics.

The results are essentially tight: W[1]-hardness and ETH-based lower bounds of n^{Omega(d)} poly(N) match the naive enumeration upper bounds (n^{O(d)} poly(N) for 2-layer networks, n^{O(d^{-1})} for zonotopes), which settles the parameterized complexity 'almost completely' and is a strong form of contribution for theory papers.

The core reduction from MULTICOLORED CLIQUE (spike/penalty function construction over Sidon sets) is clean, well-illustrated, and carefully engineered to keep the input dimension linear in the clique size — the technically non-trivial part of parameterized reductions. The homogenization gadget allowing bias-free networks is a nice reusable trick.

Broad coverage of consequences from one construction: NP- and W[1]-hardness for positivity, surjectivity, max-approximation, zero-function checking for 3-layer networks, zonotope non-containment, and Lp-Lipschitz constant computation for all p in (0, inf] — the latter extending known NP-hardness (Virmaux & Scaman only covered L2, 2-layer) to all p.

Includes genuinely positive results beyond hardness: poly-time L1 and O(2^d) L_infinity algorithms for input convex networks (Proposition 6.3), and a randomized FPT-approximation for norm maximization on zonotopes via subspace embeddings (Theorems 7.1-7.2), which provide constructive guidance and delimit where hardness stops.

The hardness is robust in a practically meaningful sense: constructions use only a constant number of non-zero weights per neuron with polynomially bounded values, so sparsity/weight-size assumptions do not circumvent intractability.
Appendix proofs are detailed, self-contained, and appear technically sound; the paper is clearly written with good figures and honest limitations discussion.
weaknesses: A substantial portion of the results are direct consequences of a single core reduction combined with previously known equivalences (e.g., the zonotope containment result is almost immediately implied by Theorem 4.2 plus the Froese et al. 2025b duality, as acknowledged in the B.6 proof which is three lines). The novelty is thus concentrated in one gadget plus extensions, which slightly limits the breadth of new technical ideas.

Purely theoretical contribution with worst-case flavor; the paper itself concedes that it provides no general guidance on which natural structural assumptions would render the problems tractable, and the relevance to real-world (trained, low-dimensional input) networks remains speculative.

The paper leaves the key classification incomplete in places it explicitly motivates: no evidence is given that the problems are in W[1] (membership left open), the Lp-maximization case for p in (1, inf) is left open, and L0 complexity is open. While these are honestly stated, they mean the parameterized complexity is not fully settled.

The randomized FPT-approximation results (Theorems 7.1-7.2) are largely derived from known subspace embedding results (Cohen & Peng 2015) and observations (Bozzai et al. 2023); the implied running time is worse than existing sampling-based approximations (Shenmaier 2018), limiting their standalone significance.

No lower bound on the running time dependence on network width n beyond the exponent; whether O(n^{cd}) with c < 1 is achievable remains open, so the 'essential optimality' claim is only w.r.t. the exponent d in the base n.

The hardness thresholds involve subtle numeric separations (e.g., 1/8 and 1/4 spike widths, epsilon scaling) whose correctness relies on Sidon set properties and bounding arguments; while the proofs appear sound, some steps (e.g., the claim that every maximizer satisfies |x_i^*| <= a_n after y-coefficient scaling) would benefit from more explicit verification, and there is no empirical or verification-tool-assisted check of the constructions.

strengths: Resolves several explicitly posed open problems from Froese et al. (COLT '25 open problem session): W[1]-hardness of 2-layer ReLU positivity (hence zonotope non-containment) parameterized by dimension d, parameterized status of Lipschitz constant computation, and injectivity of deeper networks.

The results are essentially tight: the paper pairs hardness results (W[ℓ−1]-hardness w.r.t. d, W[t]-hardness w.r.t. ℓ) with matching XP upper bounds and ETH-based running time lower bounds (n^{Ω(d)}, n^{Ω(ℓ)}, and even n^{Ω((ℓ+d)^2/4)}-type bounds via Corollary 9.4), showing that naive enumeration algorithms are essentially optimal. Table 1 gives a clear and comprehensive complexity landscape.

The core reduction (Section 4) is technically elegant: using Sidon sets (Lemma 4.3) to ensure input dimension depends only linearly on the clique size is a genuinely novel gadget design, since standard NP-hardness reductions do not control the dimension. The homogenization technique (Definition 5.1, Lemma 5.2) for removing biases is a clean and reusable tool.

The observation that the W-hierarchy aligns with ReLU network depth ('ReLU-hierarchy') is a conceptually interesting bridge between parameterized complexity and neural network theory that may spur further research.

The paper is not purely negative: it provides meaningful positive results, including polynomial-time algorithms for input-convex networks (L1 case), FPT for L∞ with respect to d, a randomized FPT-approximation for norm maximization on zonotopes via ℓ1-subspace embeddings, and sharp tractability/intractability boundaries (e.g., injectivity FPT for 2 layers but W-hard for 3).

Writing is clear and well-structured; proofs are detailed, self-contained, and include helpful illustrations (Figures 1-9); related work, including overlapping independent concurrent works, is handled transparently and fairly.
weaknesses: The parameterized classification is not fully complete: the 2-layer case is only known to lie in W[P] (not any finite level W[t]), and W[ℓ−1]-hardness is not matched by containment in W[ℓ−1]. The authors acknowledge this, but it means the 'precise' W-hierarchy characterization remains open, which slightly weakens the headline claim of settling the complexity 'almost completely'.

Part of the contribution overlaps with independent concurrent works (Cao et al., Das et al., Dewasurendra & Jayawardhana, 2026) proving W[1]-hardness of Lp-norm maximization on zonotopes; the paper's novel content for that specific sub-problem is reduced, even though the authors properly cite these works and their broader contributions (depth stratification, ETH lower bounds) remain distinct.

The results are worst-case hardness statements about arbitrary (adversarially constructed, very sparse, small-weight) networks; the connection to networks arising in practice is discussed but remains speculative, and the paper itself concedes it offers little guidance for practitioners beyond motivating heuristics and special architectures.

Several proofs (especially the odd-ℓ case in Theorem 5.4 and the Lipschitz separation arguments in Theorems 7.3-7.4) involve intricate case analyses with small-constant bookkeeping (ε-separations, fan-in bounds) that are error-prone and demand careful verification; a few steps are asserted to be 'straightforward' or 'analogous' rather than fully spelled out.

The surrogate oracle assumption for Lp-norm comparison in the Lipschitz problems (Section 2.1) is standard but slightly abstracts away bit-complexity issues for non-rational p, which could be stated more carefully.

strengths: Resolves explicit open problems posed by Froese et al. at COLT '25 (parameterized complexity of ReLU Positivity, Surjectivity, Lipschitz constant w.r.t. d, and zonotope containment), which is a significant and clearly relevant contribution to the intersection of parameterized complexity and machine learning.

Technically strong and comprehensive results: W[ℓ−1]-hardness w.r.t. input dimension, W[t]-hardness w.r.t. depth for all finite W-hierarchy levels, coW-hardness for zonotope non-containment and injectivity, all accompanied by matching ETH-based running-time lower bounds that certify the n^{(ℓ−1)d} enumeration algorithms as essentially optimal.

Careful containment side (Theorems 3.5, 3.6) placing the problems in W[P] with explicit certificates, which shows the paper is not merely a collection of hardness results but genuinely maps the parameterized complexity landscape; Table 1 gives a clean overview of near-complete settledness.

The core reduction (Proposition 4.1) is elegant and technically non-trivial: the Sidon-set/gadget construction enforces that input dimension scales only linearly with clique size, which is the key difficulty for parameterized reductions; the homogenization trick (Lemma 5.2) to remove biases is a nice reusable tool.

Includes positive results balancing the hardness picture: polynomial-time algorithms for L1-Lipschitz constant of ICNNs, FPT for L∞, and a randomized FPT-approximation for norm maximization on zonotopes via subspace embeddings (Section 8), which broadens the paper's impact beyond pure hardness.

Well-written and well-organized; proofs are detailed, self-contained, and appear correct; the conceptual link between the W-hierarchy (bounded weft) and ReLU network depth is an interesting contribution that may seed follow-up work.
weaknesses: Part of the contribution is diminished by concurrent independent work: W[1]-hardness of Lp-norm maximization on zonotopes for p ∈ (1,∞) is claimed in parallel arXiv papers (Cao et al., Das et al., Dewasurendra and Jayawardhana), so that portion is no longer novel even if independent.

Several results are hardness-only without membership at the matching level: e.g., 2-Layer ReLU Positivity is only shown in W[P], not W[1], and the ℓ ≥ 3 case lacks even W[P] membership; the complexity is thus 'almost' but not completely settled for several problems, and the W[ℓ−1]-completeness question remains open.

Much of the paper (Sections 5.4, 9) is built on top of a single reduction skeleton; while each instantiation requires non-trivial work, a reader may perceive a degree of repetitiveness across the many corollaries and derived hardness statements.

Section 8 (norm maximization via zonotope order reduction) is largely an adaptation of known subspace embedding results (Cohen–Peng, Bozzai et al.) and yields a randomized algorithm that is worse in worst-case bounds than existing sampling-based approximations (Shenmaier); its contribution is modest.

As a purely theoretical negative-results paper, the practical guidance is limited: the authors themselves concede in the conclusion that it is 'not easy to formulate a general guidance to circumvent this hardness in practice,' and there are no experiments (understandable for a theory paper, but relevant to an AI-conference audience).

Minor presentation issues: a few typos and slightly informal statements (e.g., the definition of q-norms for p ∈ (0,1) in the Lipschitz analysis, occasional awkward phrasing), though these do not affect correctness.

strengths: Resolves several explicit open problems posed by Froese et al. at COLT '25, including W[1]-hardness of 2-Layer ReLU Positivity and Zonotope Non-Containment parameterized by input dimension d, and FPT-intractability of injectivity for deeper networks. Settling open problems from a recognized venue is a clear and meaningful contribution.

The results are comprehensive and well-organized: a full picture of the parameterized complexity landscape (parameters d and ℓ) for positivity, surjectivity, Lipschitz constant computation, zonotope containment, injectivity, convexity, and network equivalence, summarized in an informative results table with theorem numbers.

A technically strong central contribution: the ETH-based lower bounds n^{Ω(d)}·poly(N) match the brute-force enumeration upper bounds n^{(ℓ−1)d}·poly(N), showing that simple enumeration algorithms are essentially optimal under ETH. The refined joint lower bound N^{Ω((ℓ+d)^2)} in Corollary 9.4 is a nice touch that closes a subtle gap between per-parameter and combined-parameter bounds.

The main reduction (Section 4) is clever and nontrivial: the use of Sidon sets to make input dimension depend only linearly on the clique size (a genuine obstacle for parameterized reductions), plus spike/penalty gadgets, is elegant and reusable. The 'homogenization' construction (Definition 5.1, Lemma 5.2) for removing biases while preserving positivity/surjectivity is a neat technical tool.

The paper establishes a conceptual connection between the W-hierarchy (weft-bounded Boolean circuits) and bounded-depth ReLU networks via W[ℓ−1]-hardness for ℓ-layer networks, which is a genuinely interesting structural insight that may seed further research.

Not purely negative: the paper provides positive results (polynomial-time L1 and 2^d·poly(N) L∞ Lipschitz computation for input-convex networks, W[P]-membership via short certificates, randomized FPT-approximation for norm maximization on zonotopes via subspace embeddings), giving a balanced picture.

Proofs are detailed, self-contained, and carefully written, with correctness arguments for all gadgets and clear handling of edge cases (e.g., zero biases, boundary points, ε-separations in the Lipschitz reductions). Reproducibility of the mathematical results is high.
weaknesses: The hardness results are matched by W[P]-membership rather than membership at the corresponding W[ℓ−1] levels, so the 'ReLU-hierarchy vs. W-hierarchy' question is left open; this limits how cleanly the depth-to-W-hierarchy connection can be interpreted, and the authors acknowledge this. The paper is therefore a near-complete but not full settlement of the parameterized complexity.

Part of the contribution (W[1]-hardness and FPT-approximation for Lp-norm maximization on zonotopes) overlaps with several concurrent independent works (Cao et al. 2026, Das et al. 2026, Dewasurendra & Jayawardhana 2026), which reduces the marginal novelty of those specific results, even though the core verification/injectivity/containment results remain distinct.

All main results are hardness results; the practical guidance for circumventing the hardness (Section 10) is necessarily vague, and the paper offers no empirical validation that the parameterized view (e.g., low input dimension) matters for networks used in practice. Significance to the mainstream AI audience rests on the relevance of low-dimensional inputs and shallow networks.

The model assumes exact real arithmetic and an oracle for Lp-norm comparisons in the Lipschitz problems; while standard for this line of work, the paper could discuss more explicitly how bit-complexity issues (weight encoding size, ε-separations that may be tiny) affect the applicability of the lower bounds to floating-point implementations.

The surjectivity-in-contrast result (P for d=1 vs. NP-hardness for d=2) and the digit-decoding construction in Theorem 9.1 introduce additional machinery whose presentation is dense; a few steps (e.g., correctness of the layer-padding argument, the ε/4 vs. 1−ε bookkeeping in Case II) require careful reader verification and would benefit from more explicit checking or an appendix.

Scope of W-hardness for parameter ℓ is via SAT-style formulas and primarily for problems derived from positivity; the ℓ-parameter results for the zonotope problems are essentially absent (marked grey in Table 1), so the ℓ-axis of the landscape is less complete than the d-axis.
